newsitem.title: USA: Precious metals soar, oil prices mostly lower.
newsitem.headline: Precious metals soar, oil prices mostly lower.

text.p: Precious metals prices rose Thursday led by platinum and palladium, which jumped higher due to a threatened strike in Russia that could cut shipments from that nation.
Workers at Russia's giant Norilsk mine have threatened to strike from March 15 over pay arrears. Norilsk is a top world supplier of cobalt, nickel and the platinum group metals.
Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium, which used in electronic components. Platinum is essential in the manufacturing of catalytic converters for automobiles.

April platinum at the New York Mercantile Exchange closed up $9.60 an ounce at $396.30 after setting a four-month high at $399.80. In the physical market, platinum was quoted at $393.50 in London, the highest level since Sept. 9, after gaining about 10 percent in the past month.

June palladium closed up $7.20 an ounce at $157.45, after setting a new life-of-contract high at $159.25. In the physical market, palladium was fixed at $157.00 an ounce, the highest price since July 11, 1995.
CPM Group metals analyst Ted Kempf pointed to two factors for the surge in the platinum group.

"The first is the increasing realisation that Russian exports of platinum and palladium to Japanese manufacturers have been interrupted and this is forcing platinum and palladium users to go to the market for the metal they need and is lending upside support to prices," Kempf said.

In December, the annual Russia-Japan supply contract talks broke down and no supplies of Russian palladium are seen likely in March for Japanese manufacturers. This has led to speculation that Japan would bid for South African supplies.

"The second explanation is that the first delivery day for the March palladium contract is on March 3 and those individuals who had sold the March contract short are hustling to offset their positions prior to that date," he said.

Buoyed by the platinum group gains, April gold futures at the Nymex's Comex division ended up $5.00 an ounce at $361.40, a 36-day high. But gold ran into heavy selling from bullion banks and producers on the run-up, traders said.
May silver futures ended up 4.7 cents an ounce at $5.295.
Oil prices closed mostly lower, with April crude oil on the Nymex ending down 22 cents a barrel at $20.89 and March heating oil down 0.65 cent a gallon at 56.03 cents.
"It looks like heating oil led the move. The weather seems to continue above normal, so we should be in this downtrend for the next month," said trader Mike De Luca at Prudential Securities.
Besides poor heating oil demand, heavy refinery maintenance has cut crude usage when gasoline demand is in a seasonal trough before steady demand in the spring and summer.
March unleaded gasoline ended 0.41 cent a gallon higher at 62.67 cents, but most gasoline contracts closed lower.
The downtrend in oil prices has lasted for about a month due to mild winter weather, lopping 20 percent off crude and heating oil prices.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, late selling by speculators and commercial grain firms pushed soybeans lower. May soybeans closed 1-1/2 cent per bushel lower at $7.84.
Traders said the soybean harvest was progressing in South America and hedge selling in futures had increased by commercial firms to lock in prices.
March soybean oil closed up 0.11 cent per pound at 24.00 cents and traders said they expected up to 2,000 lots to be posted on Friday on first notice day for cash deliveries.
March corn closed up 3-1/4 cents per bushel at $2.96 and March wheat down 2-1/2 cents per bushel at $3.68-1/4.
